paragraphs: Historians who write in aristocratic ages usually trace every event back to the particular will or temperament of certain individuals, and they tend to attribute the most important revolutions to very slight accidents. They follow the smallest causes with great shrewdness and often fail to notice the greatest. Historians who live in democratic ages show exactly the opposite tendencies. Most of them attribute hardly any influence to the individual over the destiny of the human race, or to citizens over the fate of a people. On the other hand, they assign great general causes to every petty incident. These opposite tendencies explain each other.

When the historian of aristocratic ages looks over the theater of the world, he immediately sees a very small number of leading actors who manage the whole play. These great figures stand at the front of the stage, and they catch his attention and hold it. While the historian is intent on uncovering the secret motives that make them speak and act, he forgets the rest. The importance of what some men are seen to do gives him an exaggerated idea of the influence one man can have. It naturally leads him to think that, to explain the impulses of the multitude, he must trace them back to the particular influence of some one individual.

When, on the contrary, all the citizens are independent of one another and each of them is individually weak, no one is seen to exercise great power over the community, much less lasting power. At first sight, individuals seem to have no influence over it at all, and society seems to advance by itself, through the free and voluntary cooperation of all the men who make it up. This naturally pushes the mind to look for the general reason that acts on the faculties of so many men at the same time and turns them all in the same direction at once.

I am fully convinced that even among democratic nations, the genius, vices, or virtues of certain individuals slow down or speed up the natural course of a people’s history. But causes of this secondary and accidental kind are infinitely more varied, more hidden, more complex, less powerful, and therefore harder to trace in periods of equality than in ages of aristocracy. In an aristocratic age the historian’s task is simply to pick out, from the mass of general events, the particular influences of one man or a few men. In a democratic age the historian is soon worn out by the labor, and his mind gets lost in the maze. Unable to discern clearly, or to point out plainly, the influence of individuals, he denies that it exists. He prefers to talk about the characteristics of a race, the physical features of the country, or the genius of civilization. This shortens his own labor and satisfies his reader far better at less cost.

M. de Lafayette says somewhere in his “Memoirs” that the exaggerated system of general causes offers surprising consolations to second-rate statesmen. I will add that it consoles second-rate historians just as much. It can always supply a few mighty reasons to get them out of the most difficult part of their work. It indulges the laziness or incapacity of their minds, while it gives them credit for deep thinking.

For my part, I am of the opinion that at all times one large portion of the events of this world is due to general facts and another to particular influences. These two kinds of cause are always at work; only their proportion varies. General facts explain more things in democratic ages than in aristocratic ones, and fewer things can then be assigned to particular influences. In periods of aristocracy the reverse holds: particular influences are stronger and general causes weaker, unless we count as a general cause the very fact of the inequality of conditions, which allows some individuals to thwart the natural tendencies of all the rest. Historians who try to describe what happens in democratic societies are therefore right to assign much to general causes and to give most of their attention to finding them. But they are wrong to deny entirely the particular influence of individuals just because they cannot easily trace or follow it.

Historians who live in democratic ages are not only inclined to assign a great cause to every incident; they are also inclined to connect incidents with one another so as to draw a system from them. In aristocratic ages the attention of historians is constantly drawn to individuals, so the connection between events escapes them, or rather, they do not believe in any such connection. To them the thread of history seems to be crossed and broken at every moment by the footstep of man. In democratic ages, on the contrary, the historian sees much more of actions than of actors, and so he can easily establish some kind of sequence and methodical order among the actions. Ancient literature is so rich in fine historical writing, yet it does not contain a single great historical system, while the poorest of modern literatures are full of them. It seems that the ancient historians did not make enough use of the general theories that our historical writers are always ready to carry to excess.

Those who write in democratic ages have another, more dangerous tendency. When the traces of individual action on nations are lost, it often happens that the world keeps moving although the agent that moves it can no longer be found. It becomes extremely difficult to discern and analyze the reasons that act separately on the will of each member of the community and in the end combine to set the whole mass in motion. Men are therefore led to believe that this movement is involuntary, and that societies unconsciously obey some superior force ruling over them. But even when the general fact that governs the private will of every individual is supposed to have been discovered on earth, the principle of human free will is not safe. A cause wide enough to affect millions of men at once, and strong enough to bend them all together in the same direction, may well seem irresistible. Having seen that mankind does yield to it, the mind is close to concluding that mankind cannot resist it.

Historians who live in democratic ages, then, not only deny that the few have any power to act on the destiny of a people. They also deprive the people themselves of the power to change their own condition, and they subject them either to an inflexible Providence or to some blind necessity. According to them, each nation is indissolubly bound by its position, its origin, its precedents, and its character to a certain lot that no effort can ever change. They link generation to generation. Going back in this way from age to age and from necessity to necessity, all the way to the origin of the world, they forge a close and enormous chain that girds and binds the human race. It is not enough for them to show what events have occurred; they want to show that events could not have occurred otherwise. They take a nation that has reached a certain stage of its history and assert that it could not have failed to follow the track that brought it there. It is easier to make such an assertion than to show how the nation might have taken a better course.

When you read the historians of aristocratic ages, and especially those of antiquity, it seems that to be master of his lot and to govern his fellow creatures, a man needs only to be master of himself. When you read the historical works our age has produced, it seems that man is utterly powerless over himself and over everything around him. The historians of antiquity taught how to command; those of our time teach only how to obey. In their writings the author often appears great, but humanity is always small. Suppose this doctrine of necessity, which is so attractive to those who write history in democratic ages, passes from authors to their readers, until it infects the whole mass of the community and takes possession of the public mind. It will soon paralyze the activity of modern society and reduce Christians to the level of the Turks. I would observe, moreover, that such principles are especially dangerous at the point we have now reached. Our contemporaries are only too inclined to doubt human free will, because each of them feels himself hemmed in on every side by his own weakness. But they are still willing to acknowledge the strength and independence of men united in society. Let us not lose sight of this principle, for the great goal in our time is to raise the faculties of men, not to complete their prostration.
